reports.title: Why 40% of AI agents will fail — and the four-tier fix.
reports.standfirst: Gartner expects four in ten enterprises to demote or decommission autonomous AI agents by 2027. The cause is not the agents. It is treating governance as a switch — locked down or fully trusted — instead of a dial.
reports.summary: Binary governance is the failure mode. A four-level autonomy taxonomy (Observe, Advise, Act with approval, Act autonomously) lets controls scale with what an agent can actually do.
reports.next_move: Pick one AI agent or automation already running in your business. Write down which of the four levels it sits at, what it can read, what it can write, and who owns it. If any of those four answers takes more than a minute, that is the governance gap, and it is where the first control goes.

grades.claim: 40% of enterprises will demote or decommission AI agents by 2027.
grades.note: Gartner, Inc. announcement, 26 May 2026. A forecast, not a measurement: it predicts behaviour, so it should be read as an analyst projection.

grades.claim: Binary governance is the root cause of agent failure.
grades.note: Quoted from Shiva Varma, Senior Director Analyst at Gartner, in the same announcement. An expert view supported by the two failure modes it describes.

grades.claim: Four autonomy levels: Observe, Advise, Act with approval, Act autonomously.
grades.note: A classification, not a finding. Its value is that controls can be attached to each level and stack as autonomy increases.

grades.claim: A circuit breaker should trip at a 2% error rate.
grades.note: The 2% is a worked example in the report, not a tested threshold. Set the real number from your own baseline error rate.

reports.title: The missing middle: everyday UK business workflows ready for AI.
reports.standfirst: Where is the real AI opportunity for UK businesses? Not in the boardroom and not in the chatbot, but in the overstuffed inbox, the duplicate payment and the broken hand-off between two systems nobody owns.
reports.summary: The practical AI openings in UK firms sit in everyday workflows: inbox triage, invoice matching, scheduling and the hand-offs between systems that still run on people and paper.
reports.next_move: List the five tasks in your business that someone does by hand every single day because two systems do not talk to each other. Those five are the missing middle, and the first one on the list is the pilot.

reports.title: The small business AI blind spot.
reports.standfirst: Adoption is growing. Understanding and oversight need to catch up. A widely shared headline claimed 90% of small firms use AI and only 23% understand it. We traced both figures.
reports.summary: The 90% figure is not substantiated. The 23% is real but measures formal review of in-house AI, not understanding. The useful question is what AI can access, what it costs and who owns it.
reports.next_move: Ask five business owners one question this week: could you list every AI tool your staff used last month, and what each one can access? If none can answer in under a minute, the opening is real.

grades.note: No survey, dataset or method is given for this figure in the article that carried it. Treat it as a slogan, not a statistic.
Pax8 Q3 2026 SMB AI Pulse Report, UK sample of 350. The figure is about documented review of internally built AI, not about understanding AI in general.

grades.claim: 51% of UK small firms (10–49 staff) handling digitised data use AI.
grades.note: UK Business Data Survey 2026. Different population and question from Pax8; the two cannot be combined.

grades.claim: There is a paid service in mapping a firm's AI inventory.
grades.note: What is in use, what it can reach, what it costs, who signs for it. Unproven until a customer pays for it.
